| Curriculum
Increasing inquiry and collaboration: a faculty and 
undergraduate curricular intern partnership to redesign a cell 
biology laboratory course
Louise E. O. Darling,1,2 Sarah Pociask,3John W. Goss,1,2 Julie A. Roden1,2
AUTHOR AFFILIATIONS See affiliation list on p. 11.
ABSTRACT Recent trends in undergraduate biology education include incorporating 
more inquiry/research-focused experiments into laboratory courses as a way to engage 
students and promote persistence in science. However, many faculty members face 
constraints in redesigning curricula, including a lack of time for course development. 
In addition, some undergraduate students find it difficult or intimidating to identify a 
first independent research position. We describe our experience working with student 
curricular interns to redesign a cell biology laboratory to be more inquiry-based. 
Students enrolled in the redesigned course felt that their course research experience 
was authentic and self-reported improvement in many fundamental scientific skills. 
Moreover, participating in the redesign project had positive effects on our curricular 
interns’ experiences by exposing them to independent research, pedagogical design, 
and near-peer teaching. Thus, we believe that developing ways to introduce inquirybased learning into curricula as a collaborative effort with undergraduate curricular 
interns has benefits for enrolled students, curricular interns, and faculty. We encourage 
other undergraduate science faculty to consider this model as they revise their courses.
KEYWORDS inquiry-based, undergraduate research experience, pedagogy, laboratory 
curricular development, near-peer teaching
P
reparation of students for careers in science, technology, engineering, and math 
(STEM) is a major role of a college science educator. Although United States college 
degree recipients are becoming more reflective of the diversity of the country, some 
racial/ethnic groups are still underrepresented at the bachelor’s level and higher as 
of 2021 (1). To increase retention of all undergraduates in STEM majors, a group of 
faculty proposed a “persistence framework,” including building learning communities, 
incorporating active learning into introductory classes, and early exposure to scientific
research (2). These ideas tightly align with the Vision and Change: A Call for Action final
report, focused on biological sciences, which promotes student-centered learning and

creating and sustaining communities of scholars as key tenets to transform undergraduate biology education (3).
Pedagogical innovations that support these frameworks include course-based 
undergraduate research experiences (CUREs), which include scientific practices, 
discovery, broad relevance, and opportunities for collaboration and iteration, and 
inquiry-driven laboratories, which are similar, but instructors may already know 
experimental outcomes (4). Students in one CURE laboratory course reported more 
collaboration, self-confidence, and positive attitudes toward research compared to 
students enrolled in a traditional course (5). Additionally, participation in a CURE-based 
course early in undergraduate education can improve graduation rates in STEM (6). 
However, there are some barriers to faculty redesigning a laboratory course to include

inquiry-based features, including the time it takes to design and test experiments, the 
financial cost, and, for some instructors and institutions, the lack of student preparation 
for this type of coursework (7–9). Modifying pre-existing CURE curricula for the needs of 
a particular institution’s student body is one way to facilitate this transition.
Participation in undergraduate research has been shown to increase persistence 
of students in STEM majors, particularly students from underrepresented groups (10). 
However, at undergraduate-focused institutions, it can be difficult for students to find a 
first research opportunity. In a multi-institutional survey of undergraduates, one barrier 
for students who want to do research but have not yet started is a perceived lack of 
research readiness (11). Students of color can face additional challenges to beginning 
research, including lack of representation, lack of family/community experience and

support, financial pressure, weaker academic preparation, and institutional systems 
(reviewed in reference 12). Additionally, some students describe the need to earn money 
as one reason they are considering leaving an undergraduate research experience (13). 
Alternative but authentic research opportunities might help to reduce some of these 
barriers. Research experiences related to pedagogy, such as a materials science summer 
research project in which undergraduates created a 3D printed colorimeter for use in 
introductory chemistry classes, have benefits for both undergraduate researchers and 
students in the corresponding courses (14). Pedagogical research experiences can help 
students develop “scientific research capital,” since students who have had prior research 
experience know more of the unwritten rules for finding the next research opportunity 
(15).
Involving near-peer mentoring and teaching into courses impacts enrolled students, 
the teaching/learning assistants, and the faculty instructors. At one institution, upper 
undergraduate teaching assistants (UTAs) for an introductory biology lab course who 
also enrolled in a pedagogical course designed to support their teaching felt more 
positive about instruction and more confident in writing lesson plans (16). Moreover, 
when undergraduates helped develop mathematics active learning activities and led 
these activities during a summer camp for high school students, these undergraduates 
described positive impacts on their career plans and confidence in their teaching 
ability (17). One model of a successful collaboration between a UTA and a faculty 
member incorporated ongoing course observations and conversation between both 
partners, flexibility in roles and responsibilities, and the desire to learn from each other 
(18). However, these opportunities incorporated undergraduate assistants solely into 
pedagogy and not into developing and piloting course-based research experiences.
In this study, we describe a revision of our cell biology laboratory in collaboration 
with undergraduate interns, which not only made our laboratories more inquiry-based 
but also allowed interns to conduct independent research and engage with pedagogical 
design. Our previous laboratory consisted of two “cookbook” units, where all students 
completed the same procedure and had minimal opportunity for practice or input into 
experimental design. Incorporating the principles of backward design in developing a 
CURE (19), we established goals for the revision, which were to:
• incorporate more inquiry- and student-designed and -driven research to engage

students and reflect best scientific practices,
• scaffold skills instruction to support students with different prior experiences,
• facilitate collaboration and inclusion through increased group work structure, and
• provide undergraduate internship opportunities for research and curricular 
development.
In this study, we describe the impacts that incorporating undergraduate curricular 
interns in the redesign, testing, and implementation of a CURE-based cell biology 
course based on these goals had on the enrolled students, the interns, and the 
instructors.

Intended audience
Faculty and student partners in any STEM discipline planning to revise laboratory 
curricula to introduce or augment student inquiry and research experiences are the 
intended audience for this work.
Learning time
This strategy of curricular revision with interns can be utilized for laboratories of any 
length but is particularly beneficial for faculty looking to revise or introduce multi-week, 
inquiry-based/CURE pedagogy into teaching laboratories. For curricular internships, we 
have collaborated with student curricular interns both during the academic year as a 5–
10 h per week commitment or as a 35 h per week, 9 week summer research experience.
Prerequisite student knowledge
We recommend that curricular interns have previously completed the course for which 
they will serve as redesign assistants. In our case, our curricular interns were third and 
fourth year students who had all completed the relevant coursework within the past 2 
years.
Learning objectives
By the end of this redesign process, enrolled students in a revised laboratory course will
• experience the practice of scientific research in a course-based laboratory format 
and
• develop confidence and comfort in their technical and analytical skills.
By the end of this redesign process, curricular interns will
• experience independent scientific research, including protocol development, 
troubleshooting, engaging with scientific literature, and scientific communication,
• develop confidence and comfort in their independent research skills,
• share their knowledge with less advanced students either in person or in written 
documents, and
• reflect on the role this experience had on their academic and career trajectories.
PROCEDURE
Materials

• Published CURE/inquiry-based curricula for modification and/or a novel experimental question that can be developed into a course-based research project.
• Team of instructional staff and students developing the project.
• Laboratory and meeting space to facilitate collaborative course design.
Faculty instructions
In order to revise laboratory curricula, faculty can consider either designing a new 
research project or identifying and modifying previously published CURE curricula based 
on the goals of the revision. We partnered with undergraduate curricular interns to 
adapt, extend, and pilot published curricula to better fit our student population and 
course goals and objectives. For the project described here, our goals were to increase 
student inquiry, quantitative skills, and additional exposure to fundamental cell biology 
methods and techniques for the laboratory portion of an intermediate cell biology 
course. For the first half of the semester, we adapted a laboratory series focused on 
factors impacting the yeast mating pathway in Saccharomyces cerevisiae (20). In the 
second portion of the semester, we modified our preexisting “cookbook” study of the 
apoptosis pathway in mammalian cell culture to allow student groups to have increased

agency, inspired by two other curricula (21, 22). While students used the same assays to 
examine outcomes, groups selected which chemicals they tested and at what concentrations. Current pedagogical resources for these two units are available upon request.
Over 2 years, a team of instructors and undergraduate curricular interns tested 
experiments, created pedagogical materials, and incorporated interns’ own advice to 
future students into both laboratory series (Table 1). All pedagogical materials used by 
enrolled students that were co-created by interns included authorship information. A 
subset of the interns participated in a second semester of the internship, serving as 
teaching assistants during laboratory sessions and meeting with instructors weekly to 
prepare for teaching.
Suggestions for determining student learning
We used several instruments to determine the effect of this revision process on both 
enrolled students and interns. Curricular interns who worked on either or both of the

series revisions and students enrolled in the course in Spring 2024 were invited to 
complete anonymous electronic surveys in Spring 2024 to collect information about 
their experiences (Appendices 1 and 2). Enrolled student participation was incentivized 
by awarding extra credit (0.3% of the overall course grade) to students. No compensation was provided to curricular interns for survey completion. All 46 enrolled students 
completed the survey, and 3 of 5 (60%) of the interns responded. Learning experience 
reflection (LER) course evaluations (Appendix 3) are administered to all courses at our 
institution by the registrar, and all 46 enrolled students completed this form, providing 
a second data set. Our third method of assessment was an analysis of student experimental design reflection responses that were part of the 2024 assigned coursework 
(Appendix 4), completed by a subset of students (n = 33). Free responses (a total 
of 71 individual coded comments) were anonymized and coded for themes by three 
individuals, who then met to determine consensus codes.

Sample data
Examples of outcomes from students and curricular interns are provided in the 
Discussion below.
Safety issues
We believe that it is important to discuss lab safety with curricular interns before they 
begin the project and to foster dialogue about safety considerations frequently during 
their internship. Biosafety, chemical hygiene, and other safety issues will differ based 
on the curricula chosen for development/revision. We asked our curricular interns to 
complete the same training modules that we require for students working in independent research labs on our campus.
In regard to Human Subjects research, Wellesley College contracts with Brandeis 
University for Institutional Review Board (IRB) services. Use of student and intern data 
collected in this study was determined to be exempt from human subjects protections 
review by the Brandeis University IRB, under §46.101 b, Exemption 1 and 2 (2024 survey 
data) or 4 (previously collected secondary data, LERs, and assigned coursework reflection
responses).
DISCUSSION
Field testing
Our cell biology course is an intermediate-level class used to fulfill a major requirement 
by students from multiple majors (including Biological Sciences, Biochemistry, and 
Neuroscience) at a small, selective, primarily undergraduate institution. A total of 46 
students were enrolled in four laboratory sections in Spring 2024 during their second, 
third, or fourth year of college.
We worked with five curricular interns throughout the multi-year revision process. 
Interns selected via application were work-study eligible and had previously taken the 
cell biology course. We prioritized applications from students without prior research 
experience and those from socioeconomic groups underrepresented in science. We were

able to financially support curricular interns through an institutional grant from the 
Howard Hughes Medical Institute. Curricular interns each worked 5 h/week during the 
academic year and/or 35 h/week for a 9 week summer session on curricular revisions. The 
paid internship included experimental work in the laboratory including experimental 
design and iteration, opportunities to read and discuss scientific literature, mentoring 
meetings, and whole group “lab meetings” to share data and discuss the next steps. 
Curricular interns also participated in writing/revising lab manuals and pedagogical 
materials for use in the course.
Evidence of enrolled student learning
Our primary goal for this course revision was to provide educational benefits to enrolled 
students by including more scaffolding and inquiry-based experimentation in the 
laboratory series. Most students enrolled in our revised cell biology course reported 
growth in one or more experimental/laboratory skills on our end-of-semester survey. 
At least 75% of the students cited modest to large amounts of growth in several 
skills, including developing hypotheses and experimental design (Fig. 1A). One notable 
exception was that a majority of students reported minimal to no growth in using a 
laboratory notebook, which is a skill we teach in our introductory biology courses and 
recommend students use but do not assess in this course. Many students also reported 
moderate to large gains in broader benefits such as understanding of how science works, 
readiness for more research, and tolerance of obstacles faced during research (Fig. 1B).
We also hoped to develop students’ conceptual understanding of the practice 
of science and research. The majority of student respondents (60%–70%) felt that 
both redesigned laboratory units were at least modestly like an authentic research 
Curriculum Journal of Microbiology and Biology Education
August 2025 Volume 26 Issue 2 10.1128/jmbe.00190-24 5
experience (Fig. 1C). Because both series remain somewhat constrained to allow all 
students exposure to certain techniques and for laboratory and chemical safety, we 
expected that a subset of students who were already conducting independent research 
might find the curricula limiting. As instructors, we witnessed the students’ enthusiasm 
for self-designed experiments during the semester. Several students mentioned their

enjoyment in end-of-semester survey responses, with one writing about the yeast unit 
saying, “This unit was so fun! I loved the student-designed experiment section,” and another 
discussing the apoptosis unit saying “I really liked that we were able to figure a lot of things 
out on our own [in this unit] --I feel like at that point I was confident to be more independent.” 
To better understand students’ perceptions about research, we also examined responses 
to a homework assignment after the first round of the students’ self-designed yeast 
experiment. Students discussed their plans to iterate or make changes to their protocol, 
commented on the importance of replicates or other aspects of experimental design, or 
connected their findings to their hypothesis or expected results (Fig. 2), all of which are 
key features of scientific research practices. One student specifically noted in the end of 
semester survey, “It’s unfortunate that some of the experiments/assays did not produce the 
results that were expected for each lab group, but it taught me that science is about trial and 
error - it is okay if things do not go as planned the first time around!”
Our final goal was to improve collaboration and group work during student-designed 
projects. During the revision process, instructors and curricular interns were intentional 
about creating group experimental design assignments that included guidance on 
shared responsibility, data accessibility, and other best practices. In responses from 
end-of-semester course evaluations done by the registrar, nearly all students (95%–97%) 
thought that statements that peers, instructors, and overall classroom climate were 
inclusive were very true (Fig. 3). In addition, many students reported on the student 
experience survey that they grew or developed in their ability to communicate and 
collaborate (Fig. 1A).

Evidence of curricular intern student learning
Our goals for curricular interns were to provide them with an authentic research 
experience, to help them gain confidence and experience with the practice of science, 
and to ask them to use their personal experiences to make the course more inclusive 
and accessible. We asked interns to complete an anonymous electronic survey after 
graduation, and all three intern respondents felt the internship addressed all three goals. 
Interns also had the opportunity to include free responses, and excerpts are included 
below.
First, all three curricular interns answered yes to the question “Did your HHMI 
internship feel like an authentic research experience to you?” Although our interns were 
conducting experiments that would be incorporated into teaching laboratories, because 
the two units were inquiry-based, faculty and interns were learning together and actively 
developing new protocols. Intern research experiences included both successes and 
setbacks, as described in the following comment:
Designing and piloting experiments is followed by ambiguity and repeated 
failure, which is a critical part of the research process that people considering 
research as a future career should understand. The HHMI internship was a 
valuable experience in that it exposed me to both the joys and challenges of 
research. Intern 1
Additionally, the opportunity to help create new pedagogical materials provided an 
alternative experience focused on educational practices, with one intern commenting
I was able to work closely with instructors to create materials that were actually 
used in the classroom. I was also able to get perspective on instruction and 
curriculum that I wouldn't have gotten otherwise/as a student. Intern 2
Not only did the internship feel like real research, but interns were able to build skills 
and confidence because of the structure and the scope of the project. Curricular interns 
worked as a team, with different interns working together as their schedules allowed. 
They were jointly mentored by research-active tenure-track faculty and teaching-focused 
non-tenure track faculty. In answer to the question “Did your HHMI internship change 
your comfort and competence in conducting independent research?” all three interns 
described their experiences positively:

The internship helped fill in gaps by teaching/re-teaching me critical skills 
and techniques through repeated exposure and explanation, allowing me to 
develop the confidence to perform experiments. Intern 1

As part of an ongoing initiative on our campus to make science education more

In the survey, all three interns answered positively to the question: “Did you feel like 
curricular changes you worked on would make the Cell Biology laboratory experience 
more inclusive or investigative?” One intern highlighted the collaborative nature of the 
revision process as an inclusive approach, saying
Since the team of students and professors … were also at different stages of 
their research career, every member had different perspectives to offer that 
were beneficial to creating an inclusive and investigative laboratory experience.

We have remained in touch with most of our curricular interns after their time 
working with us. All interns have completed their undergraduate degrees, and the 
majority have stayed in the biomedical field after graduation: two are working as 
research technicians, and two are currently enrolled in a graduate health degree

Additionally, before applying to a graduate health degree program, one of our interns 
spent two years as a secondary school educator. Her experience as a teaching assistant in 
Spring 2021 (Table 1) provided her with valuable insights, as she describes
Thanks to the patience and mentorship of [my faculty co-instructor], I was able 
to take what I learned from [them] as a professor and apply it in a classroom full 
of middle/high school students. Intern 3
Overall, our limited data suggest that participation in a curricular internship to 
develop an inquiry-based laboratory series can have impacts on interns’ interest in 
research, their confidence in conducting it, and their career paths after graduation. 
In addition, for interns interested in teaching and pedagogy, this type of internship 
can also provide experience not traditionally found in biology coursework or research 
experiences.
Reflections and recommendations for implementation of this model
We believe that our revision met our goals of transforming our intermediate cell biology 
laboratory course into a more inquiry-focused, collaborative experience. The majority

of enrolled students surveyed reported that they developed multiple scientific and 
technical skills over the semester. The benefits to morphing our previous “cookbook” 
style laboratories into two inquiry-based modules were similar to other published 
outcomes, including student enjoyment of research (24); the ability to discover, iterate, 
and collaborate (25); gains in self-confidence, experimental design, and other lab skills 
(5); and in understanding of research practices and challenges (23).
Curricular interns felt like their work developing the CURE laboratories was a real 
research experience and an opportunity to benefit future iterations of the course. 
However, because experiments were geared to an audience of intermediate undergraduate students, the scope and methodology of the research were significantly more 
constrained than they would be in a faculty research lab. These features allowed our 
interns to quickly develop expertise and begin designing their own experiments, some 
of which were used with permission as models for students enrolled in our course. 
Several of our interns used this research opportunity as a stepping stone to springboard 
into other research experiences either during college or after graduation.
What we as faculty found most exciting about the curricular renovations was the 
process of implementing an inquiry-based curriculum in collaboration with undergraduate interns. Benefits for the instructors included assistance with piloting and testing 
experiments, providing additional research and teaching opportunities for upper-level 
undergraduates, and identification and revision of materials that might confuse enrolled 
students. We enjoy teaching in our new inquiry-based laboratory series, as our enrolled students are more engaged and excited. The revision timeline was significantly
faster than a solely faculty-driven project because the team doing the work was larger. 
Additionally, having curricular interns pilot experiments in advance identified procedures, equipment, or other tasks that might confuse students. Interns were able to help 
revise or generate helpful resources prior to launching the curriculum for students in the 
course.
Because revisions were done as a team of curricular interns and faculty, interns had 
the opportunity to learn from each other as well as develop mentoring relationships with 
multiple faculty members. This type of model has been successful in other undergraduate research experiences, such as a team of astronomy faculty, graduate students, 
Curriculum Journal of Microbiology and Biology Education

August 2025 Volume 26 Issue 2 10.1128/jmbe.00190-24 9
postdocs, and other undergraduates working on a large project where each member 
is responsible for their own portion of the project (26) or a group of mathematicians 
and biologists creating a multi-year team-oriented interdisciplinary research experience 
in quantitative biology (27). Anecdotally, one of the faculty authors (J.A.R.) has used 
the curricular intern model in other settings at our institution, including an organismal 
biology course redesign (28) and an online introductory research immersion program 
(29) with similar positive outcomes for both faculty and interns.
We acknowledge some drawbacks and limitations to this work. Our study included a 
very small set of responses from curricular interns and students involved in one course 
redesign at a selective undergraduate institution, so conclusions drawn might not be 
applicable to students and interns from other educational backgrounds. We had financial
support to pay our curricular interns for their work, which might not be an option for 
some resource-limited institutions. We propose a research credit model as an alternative 
to provide some form of compensation for the time invested by interns. Because course 
redesign work is of limited duration (either 1–2 semesters or 1 summer in our experience), interns need to seek other opportunities after the culmination of the project if 
they hope to continue developing their research experience portfolio. Finally, although 
students in our class self-reported gains and benefits from their experience in this course, 
we did not collect outcomes from the previous “cookbook” labs to directly compare 
these courses to know if these gains were significantly larger than the prior version of the 
course.
We encourage other faculty to consider the curricular intern model as they develop 
or revise teaching laboratories to include inquiry-based elements or a full CURE in any 
experimental STEM course. We believe that this strategy of collaborating with curricular 
interns to design inquiry-based laboratories touches on key recommendations of the 
Vision and Change final report, including introducing the scientific process and exposure 
to research, focusing on student-centered learning, engaging multiple stakeholders in 
improving education and pedagogy, and ensuring access to engaging biology (3). In our 
experience, a research-based curricular development internship provides a supported

first exposure to independent research and helps interns with less “scientific research 
capital (15)” develop skills and connections to find future research opportunities. 
Therefore, we encourage faculty to consider prioritizing intern selection from students 
with backgrounds underrepresented in science. We feel that this model could also 
benefit from more sustained collaboration with colleagues in departments or schools 
of education or for STEM departments with significant numbers of graduates moving 
on to careers in education. We realized that developing/revising a laboratory series in 
collaboration with curricular interns would be an opportunity to train undergraduates 
interested in STEM education in part since one of our interns accepted a post-graduation 
job as a high school science teacher. Exposing future teachers to research is a need 
highlighted by at least one review of the CURE and other undergraduate research 
literature (30), as well as the Vision and Change Report (3). The curricular internship 
mentorship model can also provide opportunities for teaching-focused faculty and 
institutions to provide mentorship and authentic research opportunities for undergraduates, even if they do not have a pre-existing research program. We believe this model can 
be effective either as an academic year position or as a summer research opportunity, 
depending on the needs and time constraints of the faculty member(s).
